label: First playdate

what_happens.title: What happens on a playdate
goals: A friend comes to play, or we go to them
There is play, snack and tidy-up
what_happens.parentSkill: Tell your child how long the playdate lasts, using a marker like "until snack and one more game".

who_is_there.title: Who is at the playdate
goals: The friend, and maybe the friend's grown-up
who_is_there.parentSkill: Tell your child the friend's name and the grown-up's name, and where you will be.

what_i_do.title: What I do at the playdate
goals: Use words when there is a problem
what_i_do.parentSkill: Practise turn-taking with a timer or a "you choose, I choose" rule.

if_scared.title: If it feels tricky
goals: Feeling shy or cross is normal
Disagreements happen and can be fixed
Calm tools: words, a break, a grown-up
if_scared.parentSkill: Coach, don't rescue: 'You both want the truck. What could you try?'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise the playdate
goals: Practise taking turns and using words
Choose snack and special toys to put away
rehearsal.parentSkill: Play a pretend playdate with toys, including a pretend disagreement solved with words.

steps: Choose a few games and put away special toys
The friend arrives, or we go to their home
Say hello and show the toys or the garden
sensory: a friend's voice and laughter in my home
a different house with different smells
honestyNotes: Playdates can include disagreements, sharing struggles and tears; never promise it will be perfect. It is okay to put away a few special toys. Children may want to stop early. Let the parent say whose home it is and how long it lasts.

questionButtons.text: Do I have to share everything?
fallbackAnswer: You can put away a few special toys first.
For the rest, taking turns helps everyone have fun.

questionButtons.text: What if my friend doesn't like my games?
fallbackAnswer: You can ask, what do you want to play?
One game for you, one game for me.
Friends disagree sometimes. Use words, and ask a grown-up for help.
Problems can be fixed.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you if they stay, or when they come back.
A grown-up is always nearby.

questionButtons.text: What is my friend's home like?
fallbackAnswer: Every home is a bit different, with its own rules and smells.
You can ask where the toilet is and what the rules are.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you their name.
They look after you both and can help you.
Feeling shy at first is normal.
You can show your friend one toy to start.

questionButtons.text: What if I don't like their snack?
fallbackAnswer: You can say, no thank you.
There will be something else.
[[GROWNUP]] will tell you, maybe until snack and one more game.
Then it is goodbye.

questionButtons.text: What if it gets too loud?
fallbackAnswer: Playdates can get noisy with running and giggling.
You can suggest a quiet game, like drawing.

questionButtons.text: What if they play with someone else?
fallbackAnswer: You can ask, can I join?
Or suggest a game for everyone.

techniques.label: A special toy box
techniques.how: Put away a few special toys before the playdate.

techniques.label: A turn timer
techniques.how: Use a timer or counting for turns.

techniques.label: Feeling words
techniques.how: Practise: I don't like that, can I have a turn?

techniques.label: An activity plan
techniques.how: Choose two or three activities ahead of time.

techniques.label: A snack break
techniques.how: Plan a snack in the middle to reset.

techniques.label: Asking about house rules
techniques.how: Ask the friend's grown-up about rules and the toilet.

techniques.label: A five-minute warning
techniques.how: Give a five-minute warning before goodbye.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in slowly through the nose and out like blowing a candle.

ritual: Choose games and put special toys away
One for me, one for you
Tidy up and say thank you

pain: If someone gets bumped, stop and check, and say sorry.
Tell a grown-up if something hurts.
body: Snack time is a nice break.
You can say no thank you.
sensory: It's getting loud. Want a quiet game?
New homes smell different. That is normal.
strangers: That's Toby's mum. She'll look after you both.
You can ask her for help.
separation: I'll be in the kitchen if you need me.
I will come back at the end.
safety: Use your words: I don't like that.
Ask a grown-up if words don't work.
social: One for you, one for me.
Ask your friend what they want to play.
love: I'm proud of how you took turns.
I love seeing you play with friends.

A playdate is when a friend comes to play, or when we visit a friend.
First [[CHILD]] chooses some games and puts away a few special toys.
Then the doorbell rings, ding dong.
[[CHILD]] can ask the friend, what do you want to play?
Before bed, here is a story about a little otter called Olive.
Olive invited her friend Toby the turtle to play.
First Olive picked out her favourite games.
She put her special shell in a box, just for her.
Then there was a knock at the den.
Hello, Toby, said Olive.
Next they built a river of stones and floated leaf boats.
After that, they had fish crackers on the riverbank.
Then they tidied up the stones together.
Bye, Toby, said Olive, come again.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next the friends say hello and choose what to play.
After a while, there is a snack together.
Then a little more play, and tidy-up time.
Last, the friend says goodbye, and the playdate ends.

Mine, said Olive, and Toby frowned.
Then Olive remembered.
One turn for me, one turn for you, she said.
They counted to twenty for each turn.
Later, Toby splashed Olive too hard.
I don't like that, said Olive.
Sorry, said Toby, and they played gently.
At snack time they shared fish crackers.
Then they tidied up, and Toby said, thank you for having me.

In the story, Olive the otter felt shy when Toby arrived.
She hid behind her mama.
Then Toby wanted to play turtle tag, and Olive wanted boats.
Olive felt cross and wanted to cry.
Mama did not say, be nice and share everything.
Mama said, you both want different games, what could you try?
Olive took a slow breath, like smelling a flower.
Then she said, turtle tag first, then boats?
Toby grinned, okay.
They played both, and laughed.
Worried and brave can happen at the same time.
Taking a little break helps big feelings shrink.
Even good friends disagree.

Hosting means helping a guest feel welcome, like offering a choice of games and a snack.
Visiting means following that home's rules, which may be different from yours.
Friendships grow through shared play and small kindnesses.
Short playdates often go better than long ones at first.
[[CHILD]] can plan two or three activity ideas in case of a quiet moment.
Being a good guest includes asking before using things and following the house rules.
Being a good host includes letting the guest choose sometimes.
Siblings joining in can be fun or tricky; a grown-up can help balance it.
Each family has different rules about screens, snacks and where to play.
[[CHILD]] can ask the friend about their favourite things to find common ground.
Compromise, finding a game both people like, is a key friendship skill.
Saying how you feel without blaming, like I felt left out, helps solve problems.
Taking a break when tempers rise prevents bigger fights.
Thanking the guest or the host is good manners and leaves a good memory.
[[CHILD]] can suggest a game that needs two people, like building or a board game.
Friendship conflicts are normal and are how kids practise negotiation.
Feeling left out or bossed around is worth talking about afterwards.
If a friend is unkind repeatedly, a grown-up should know.
Ending a playdate early because it is not working is fine.
[[CHILD]] can think of what to try next time, like a different game or a shorter time.
Planning a few activities means no awkward, what now, moments.
Thinking about what the friend likes shows care.
Agreeing a time to finish helps everyone end on a good note.
A quick chat afterwards about what went well builds social confidence.
[[CHILD]] can write or draw a small invitation for the friend.
